## 6.9 Two priors, an elders' going and a kind's artifact

A young self opens with two priors, its elders' going and its kind's artifact. Navigating going on across generations is a society's prior same-existing: a young self opens with its elders' going as a prior other-parity, the second of the five dimensions, and that other's prior is becoming its own prior, a crane's route straightening as it learns from older cranes, a herd's migration returning over decades, a voyaging people's charts passing from father to son. A young self opens, too, with its kind's genome, an artifact of prior living whose stable form co-sequentially, geodesically aims it into healthy living, from each is-not to is. A "map", a "program", a "magnetic sense" and a "memory" going down generations are a field's store story over both.

Whooping cranes from captive breeding, an ultralight aircraft leading their first migration, go on to migrate alone or in groups; over eight years, a crane's flying route goes closer to a straight line as it learns from older birds, seven years of experience bringing a 38 percent improvement in accuracy, and genetic relatedness making no difference. In a migrating flock of young white storks, leaders fly irregular paths, searching out the rising warm air within thermals, and followers soar in more regular paths on their exploring, losing height faster between thermals and flapping more; a bird's place in the flock goes with its flying efficiency, efficient fliers going on to winter in West Africa and less efficient ones in southern Europe, a winter place foreseeable from a few minutes of flight. Bighorn sheep that people move into ranges whose earlier herds are at an end: under 9 percent of them migrate, against 65 to 100 percent in herds that stay whole; herds starting again at those ranges reaching 80 percent migrating only after nearly 40 years, and moose about 90 years, a herd's going with the spring's new growth up the slopes improving over decades, the knowledge passing from mothers and herd members to the young.

A salmon lives with its genome, an artifact of its kind's prior living, year round, in healthy living and ingesting conditions, river and ocean; that artifact's stable form co-sequentially, geodesically aims a salmon into healthy living, out to its kind's good feeding waters and home up its river at its season, from each is-not to is. Juvenile Chinook salmon from a hatchery, more than 1,000 of them, none ever in the ocean, each some eight minutes in a bucket inside a platform of copper wires making a field an instrument reads as that of the northern edge of their kind's ocean range, tend to swim south, and with the field of the far southern edge of that range, tend to swim north, toward their kind's feeding waters; in the test site's own field they swim in random directions. The researchers name it a map sense a fish inherits, a fish "programmed to know what to do": a self observing reads a young salmon's heading toward its kind's healthy feeding as one with no ocean yet of its own, its genome an artifact of its kind's prior living and its stable form aiming it. Chinook salmon and steelhead each go up their rivers in two forms, a premature form months ahead of spawning, spring Chinook and summer steelhead, and a mature form ready to spawn, fall Chinook and winter steelhead; across hundreds of thousands of genome points, one region, GREB1L, tells the two forms apart completely in both species, each species' premature form tracing to one evolutionary event of its own. A salmon's season of going home is its kind's artifact of prior living with its river's seasons, its stable form co-sequencing a salmon with its river.

A year's monarchs are an overwintering generation and three or four summer generations; monarchs coming out in late summer and early fall are biologically and behaviorally different, not mating or laying eggs until the next spring, living some eight or nine months against three to five weeks for a summer adult, going up to three thousand miles south, eastern monarchs to oyamel fir forests in central Mexico and western monarchs to California's coastal groves, often to the exact same trees, and each making the round trip once, the monarchs arriving at those trees being the great-great-grandchildren of the monarchs leaving them the spring before. No monarch going south has a prior of its own at those forests and groves: a monarch's going is its kind's artifact of prior living with milkweed and with a winter forest, its stable form aiming an autumn monarch into healthy living, and a year's generations one same-existing-society going round one year.

European eels live as adults in Europe's fresh waters and go 5,000 to 10,000 km across the Atlantic to the Sargasso Sea to spawn, eating nothing on the way, diving to about 1,500 m by day and rising to about 200 m by night, some 3 to 12 km a day, a going of perhaps 18 months; of 26 eels with satellite tags from the Azores, 23 tags giving data, six reach the Sargasso Sea, the first direct evidence of adults at the Sargasso Sea, and the eels' larvae drift back to Europe on the North Atlantic Drift. An eel's going is its kind's artifact of prior living, its stable form aiming an eel to the sea its kind's living opens at, a depth going with day and night and a larva's drift going with a current, each a co-sequencing. Loggerhead turtles nesting on beaches at which an instrument reads a like magnetic field are genetically like each other, more than turtles on beaches close to each other or of a like environment, turtles on Florida's two coasts at which an instrument reads a like field being genetically like each other too; the study's authors ask whether a turtle learns its home or its genome gives it. A self observing reads a going-with: a turtle's coming home is its kind's artifact of prior living and its own prior same-existing now-existing in it, an instrument's reading at a beach going with that from outside a turtle's surface, and learning-or-genome a store question over one artifact of living.

Each self an exploring observes lives with its kind's genome, an artifact of prior living, and that artifact shows three ways. It aims the going itself: a salmon, a monarch, a locust and an eel. It goes beside an elders' prior: a crane's route straightens as it flies with older cranes, and relatedness makes no difference; and a loggerhead's coming home, learning or genome, is open. And it parts from one self with one genome, in three cases: a mature sperm's genome lies tight and largely silent, its swimming going with proteins and a flagellum forming as a sperm is forming, its kind's prior artifact in that forming, and its own genome going on to its next, a new self it opens with an egg; a hive or an ant colony is many genomes of kin, each bee's or ant's its own and no one genome the society's, its swarming or moving house and its quorum going across many artifacts, in no genome alone; and a bobtail squid and Aliivibrio fischeri are two kinds' artifacts living as one same-existing-society, neither genome having the whole of it. A genome is an artifact of prior living going on, lineages going on to a next, and prior living going on to no next has no artifact here.

## 6.10 A hive podaling, and a society moving as its parity changes

A hive's collective intelligence is podaling: its foragers' trips out and back, away and back, go across and along the surface around a hive's now-existing, each forager with her own source and only a parity going across at a dance, and a hive is co-competencing the observings of many trips. Podaling exchanges its across and its along while each forager goes on forward, and a hive's intelligence is its surface around now-existing co-intelligencing, in no forager alone. The moment a hive moves is a moment of geodesic parity changing from now-existing here to next-existing, aiming to go in the direction of social moral competency. A hive begins moving as it is-not stable-forming here, and its moving is social abundancing: one same-existing-society opening as two, each going on forward.

In Seeley, Camazine and Sneyd's account, a honey bee forager judges only her own nectar source, its profitability, with no comparing among sources: from a richer source she works faster, dances more intensely and is less likely to abandon it, and from a poorer one the reverse, and a colony's preference for its better sources arises from these. No forager compares sources; each trip's parity goes across at a dance, and a colony's choosing is a podaling. A young bumblebee, within a day or two of coming out, flies complex loops of ever-increasing size around its colony, and with experience flies direct paths, mostly upwind on its outward trips, though forage is in each direction. Each loop, a going away and a going back on one ring, is a podal at one bee's scale, each loop reaching further across and along the surface around its colony's now-existing.

A honeybee swarm choosing its home is collective discovery by the geodesic method: a home over its horizon is, each scout finds is-nots and aims from them, each scout's sharing for a site emptying with each return as the method's is-not emptying, a stop signal sharing an is-not across, and the swarm reaching its is at the site, a quorum of its selves at that site, in no bee alone. A scout with no site yet, following a dance, flies to the site and inspects it herself, dancing for it only if she judges it worthy, and a field's account describes no bee comparing two sites side by side; in a five-box test of four 15-litre boxes and one 40-litre box, swarms settle on the best box in four of five trials, a choosing in no bee alone. Its quorum is at 3.5, and its stop signal at 3.7.

A swarm's moving begins as 15 or more bees are at one of the sites together; scouts then scramble through the cluster pressing their vibrating thoraxes against other bees, and each bee's thorax warms to about 35 °C before the swarm lifts off, a five-site test bringing a quorum much more slowly and a lifting off coming almost twice as late. The warming is a build-up and the lifting off a moment: a swarm's parity changing from now-existing in its cluster to next-existing in flight, toward the site its scouts are at, a whole society warming and going. About 3 to 4 percent of a flying swarm's bees know the new site from their own visits; these streakers fly fast through the swarm's top toward the site, then make slower flights along its rear and loop back to streak again; the fastest bees fly most directly toward the site, bees accelerate from rear to front, and followers likely latch on and chase them, a chain reaction; flights of about 270 m top out at 5 to 7 km/h and longer ones about 12 km/h.

A honey bee colony swarms as it is crowding, its population growing with no room to grow in its nest, its queen's mandibular pheromone thinning through it, open cells for laying growing few, with more nectar and pollen and longer days: the old queen goes out with some 50 to 70 percent of the workers, and the parent colony goes on with some 30 to 50 percent, all its brood and several queens developing in their cells, one of them in time going on as its queen. A colony is-not stable-forming here as one, and it opens as two, a social abundancing, each society going on forward. Ants of Temnothorax albipennis moving house: a recruiter leads one follower at a time to a new site in a tandem run while the site is relatively empty, and as enough nestmates are at it, recruiters switch to carrying the colony's passive majority, at a rate three times a tandem run's, tandem runs going on now and then in the other direction, back toward the old nest. A quorum at a new site is a colony's moment of parity changing from now-existing at its old nest to next-existing at its new one, and the tandem runs back toward the old nest are podaling, away and back, across and along.

An army ant colony, Eciton burchellii, goes in two phases with its brood: some twenty days at one bivouac, a living nest of its own hanging workers, as its pupae and new eggs develop, raiding on about alternate days; and as its eggs hatch and its pupae open, some fifteen days nomadic, raiding each day and moving its bivouac, mostly by night, six to eight hours a move. A colony stable-forms at one place as its brood develops, and as its brood opens, its next arriving within it, it is-not stable-forming at one place and goes on, a social abundancing moving it. A desert locust lives in a solitary form or a gregarious form, both in one genome; crowding on shrinking patches of plants brings the change, and in a laboratory some two hours of touching a solitary locust's hind legs, as a crowd's jostling does, brings it, its serotonin in its thorax rising about threefold for less than a day, blocking its serotonin receptors or its serotonin production preventing the change and injecting serotonin with no other locusts close bringing it; swarms go as billions over many square kilometres. A field's Jekyll and Hyde and a plague are its story over this: a locust in a crowd is-not stable-forming as solitary, and its genome's artifact has its next form ready, a society going.
